Fatal Traps & Industrial Pitfalls in Recuperated Gas Turbines

1. High Pressure Ratio Thermal Inversion (T2 > T4 Penalty)

Attempting to retrofit a recuperator onto an aeroderivative gas turbine designed with a high pressure ratio (r_p > 18–24) creates a severe thermal inversion. Compressor discharge temperature (T_2) exceeds the turbine exhaust gas temperature (T_4). Hot compressed air transfers heat into the exhaust stream instead of absorbing it, dropping cycle efficiency by 8% to 12% below simple-cycle baseline.

2. Parasitic Recuperator Pressure Drops Crippling Expansion Ratio

Every percentage of frictional pressure drop across the recuperator air side (ΔP_air/P ≈ 2.5%) and exhaust gas side (ΔP_gas/P ≈ 4.0%) directly diminishes the expansion pressure ratio across the turbine. An unoptimized heat exchanger causing a cumulative 6% gas-side backpressure robs over 10% of gross turbine shaft output, completely offsetting the thermodynamic heat recovery benefit.

3. Thermal Fatigue Cracking from Rapid Peaking Start-Up Cycles

Recuperator cores (brazed stainless steel or nickel-alloy primary-surface plate-fin matrices) have massive thermal inertia compared to lightweight turbine rotors. Fast cold starts (0 to 100% load in under 10 minutes) expose thin internal corrugations to severe differential thermal expansion stresses exceeding 350 MPa, causing weld ligament rupture, internal leakage, and rapid cross-contamination.

4. Low-Temperature Sulfuric Acid Dew Point Corrosion

When firing fuels containing trace sulfur (e.g. landfill biogas, sour natural gas, or light diesel), SO&sub2; and SO&sub3; combine with combustion water vapor. If highly effective recuperation extracts exhaust heat down below the acid dew point (typically 125°C to 140°C), concentrated sulfuric acid condenses directly on cold-end recuperator tubes, eating through stainless steel matrices in under 1,500 operating hours.

5. Cold Ambient Density Surge & Compressor Surge Margin Collapse

On sub-zero winter days (-15°C to -30°C), dense ambient air increases compressor mass flow and pressure ratio significantly. Without variable inlet guide vanes (VIGVs) and bleed valves, the compressor operating point migrates dangerously toward the aerodynamic surge line. A sudden stall or surge cycle induces severe reverse flow oscillations that shatter first-stage axial blading.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does a recuperator (regenerator) improve gas turbine thermal efficiency? +
A recuperator is a gas-to-gas heat exchanger that transfers waste heat from the hot turbine exhaust gas (typically 450°C–600°C) to preheat the high-pressure air leaving the compressor before it enters the combustor. This directly reduces the fuel required to achieve the turbine inlet temperature (TIT), increasing overall cycle thermal efficiency by 5% to 15% percentage points, especially at moderate pressure ratios (r_p = 6 to 16).
Why does recuperation become ineffective or detrimental at high pressure ratios? +
As compressor pressure ratio (r_p) increases, compressor discharge temperature (T_2) rises due to isentropic compression heating, while turbine exhaust temperature (T_4) drops due to deeper expansion. At high pressure ratios (typically r_p > 18 to 22), compressor discharge air is actually hotter than the turbine exhaust (T_2 > T_4). In this condition, an exhaust heat exchanger would cool the compressed air rather than heat it, destroying cycle efficiency.
What is the Back Work Ratio (BWR) and why is it so high in gas turbines? +
The Back Work Ratio is the fraction of total turbine mechanical power output consumed internally by the compressor: BWR = W_compressor / W_turbine. In gas turbines, BWR typically ranges from 40% to 60% because compressing gaseous air consumes vastly more work than pumping incompressible liquid water in a Rankine steam cycle (where BWR is only 1% to 2%).
How does multi-stage compressor intercooling boost net power output? +
Compressor work scales directly with inlet absolute temperature: w_c = c_p * T_in * (r_p^(k-1)/k - 1). Splitting compression into two stages with an intermediate intercooler reduces the air temperature entering the second stage, cutting total compressor work by 12% to 20%. While intercooling slightly lowers combustor air inlet temperature, pairing intercooling with a recuperator yields simultaneously higher net specific power and superior thermal efficiency.
What is Heat Rate and how does it relate to thermal efficiency? +
Heat Rate is the thermal energy input (from fuel) required to produce one kilowatt-hour of electrical or shaft energy: Heat Rate (kJ/kWh) = 3600 / eta_thermal, or in imperial units: Heat Rate (BTU/kWh) = 3412.14 / eta_thermal. Lower heat rate indicates a more fuel-efficient turbine. High-efficiency recuperated microturbines achieve heat rates near 10,000 kJ/kWh (36% efficiency), whereas simple-cycle peakers operate near 12,500–14,000 kJ/kWh (25%–28% efficiency).
